blocks.text: Everything so far assumed the array's size was fixed when it was created. That follows directly from the memory model — a contiguous block must be reserved up front, and the neighbouring memory may already belong to something else.
Yet you write `list.push(x)` every day and it simply works. This chapter builds the thing that makes that possible.

A true array cannot grow. Its block is exactly as large as requested, and the bytes immediately after it are not yours. Appending would mean writing into memory you do not own — either corrupting another value or crashing.

Step 2 is O(N). That is unavoidable — nothing can make copying N elements cheaper than N operations.
The naive version and why it is terrible
The obvious policy is to grow by exactly one slot each time. Appending N elements then costs:
Building a list of a million items would take roughly 500 billion copy operations. In practice, minutes for something that should be instant.
If growing is O(N) and unavoidable, how can `push` be considered O(1)?

The answer is not that copying is avoided — it is that copying is made **rare enough** that its cost, spread across all the cheap appends, averages out to a constant. The next lesson picks the growth policy that achieves it.
